extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians (researchers, faculty, graduate students) who write expository articles, opinion pieces, books, or letters of recommendation
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative standards for writing mathematical expository articles (surveys), opinion pieces, prefatory material, and professional letters of recommendation. Emphasizes audience-targeting, structure, evidence, bibliography, and professional candor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience targeting / know your audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide in advance the intended audience and keep that group clearly in focus; the reader of an expository article is not a research-paper reader and should not be assumed to have perfect background.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constantly measure level and style to the audience (e.g., freshmen for a calculus book, fellow researchers for a research article). The single most important attribute of an effective writer is a strong sense of the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility / reader effort
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader of an expository article should not have to work as hard as the reader of a research article; present material so a casual reader (on a park bench or with coffee) can follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assuming the reader will slog through detailed proofs; give sketches and explanations rather than full technical proofs. Use background and motivation to reduce reader effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain jargon and assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume the reader already knows all the jargon or motivations; state what you assume and what you conclude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate audience shortcomings, explain specialized terms, and give sufficient motivation and applications. Prefatory remarks should include intended prerequisites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate level of detail versus handwaving
rubrics_metrics.description: Strike a balance between how much mathematical detail to give and how much explanation or handwaving to provide; surveys generally will not present full proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing what to prove, balance instructive value against feasibility; prove special cases or add simplifying hypotheses when helpful, but be honest about the simplification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of proofs and sketches
rubrics_metrics.description: State theorems precisely and correctly but, when presenting proofs in exposition, give sketches or pseudo-proofs and declare any simplifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers appreciate nuggets of knowledge without gory details; explicitly note when you 'consider only a special case' or assume extra smoothness for simplicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization: detailed outline / Table of Contents
rubrics_metrics.description: Before writing a survey or book, prepare a detailed outline or TOC so you can see the full scope and keep the project organized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A TOC helps measure progress and prevents you from becoming confused; for large projects it is nearly essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative structure / storytelling
rubrics_metrics.description: A good survey should tell a story: build to a climax, create a tapestry rather than listing results chronologically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange historical turning points, examples, and developments to show the genesis of the subject and to lead the reader through a cohesive narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use well-chosen examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Present carefully selected examples and work them through to illustrate general reasoning; an example may show the only way something can go wrong and how hypotheses rule it out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single illustrative example can be used to indicate how a general proof works; choose examples that illuminate central ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stirring conclusion and future directions
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclude surveys by reviewing covered ground, noting historical turning points, and speculating on future milestones and directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid trivial closings; the conclusion should sum up lessons learned and where the subject might go, giving the reader a sense of closure and forward-looking perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extensive, curated bibliography
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide an extensive bibliography of your own rather than just pointing to standard texts; your bibliography defines what the subject is and which papers are most important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compiling a good bibliography is necessary work; consider providing a complete list online if journal constraints force a short printed list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preface / prefatory remarks
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a Preface or prefatory paragraphs stating why you write, your goals, what you intend to accomplish, what you assume, and who the intended audience is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Preface helps both reader and author; write a version before you begin to organize, and rewrite it at the end to reflect the finished work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty about scope and simplifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Be explicit when you simplify arguments, restrict to special cases, or assume extra hypotheses for clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State simplifications up front so readers know when a sketch omits technicalities, preventing misrepresentation of completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research to support opinion pieces
rubrics_metrics.description: An opinion piece often requires considerable research—gather facts, studies, and relevant literature to defend your thesis, not just anecdotes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best to formulate and state the thesis clearly at the outset (ideally in the first paragraph) and back it with a mix of facts, anecdotes, and logical argument appropriate to the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear thesis statement for opinion pieces
rubrics_metrics.description: State your thesis deliberately and explicitly, preferably in the first paragraph or first sentence, so the reader knows the point you will defend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-posed thesis helps structure the remainder of the piece; avoid writing without a clear, defendable position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persuasive structure and balance
rubrics_metrics.description: For persuasive writing, balance entertaining anecdotes with solid facts and logical reasoning to maintain force and reader engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pure anecdote lacks long-term convincing power; pure dry fact may fail to hold attention—mix depending on audience and subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concluding paragraph / restate and emphasize
rubrics_metrics.description: End position papers by summing up major points, repeating the most important ideas, and forcefully stating the desired conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh words carefully in the closing; treat it like a closing argument and ensure the reader leaves with the intended takeaway.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and professionalism in correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: Respond promptly to requests (accept or decline quickly) and write requested letters in a timely fashion; ask for needed information to avoid delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you cannot write (conflict of interest, unfamiliarity), inform the requester immediately. Use administrative aids (students' info slips or web forms) to collect facts and ensure timely completion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening paragraph clarity for recommendation letters
rubrics_metrics.description: In the first few sentences, state plainly the question addressed (e.g., support for tenure/promotion), how long you've known the candidate, and your overall judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the letter's purpose unmistakable up front; follow with detailed support and conclude by restating your recommendation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific evidence and scope-limited claims in recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Support your thesis with specific comments about particular work or papers; be precise and speak only of topics you know directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain importance of specific results, improvements over earlier work, publication venues, and provide background for nonspecialist evaluators. Vague praise is unhelpful and may be misread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binary comparisons in evaluation letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Make binary comparisons: situate the candidate among contemporaries (e.g., 'the five best people under 35 in this area are...') so readers understand the candidate's relative standing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare to recognizable peers of similar career stage; tailored, explicit comparisons (even a rough rank) are far more informative than vague generalities. Avoid inappropriate comparisons (e.g., junior candidate vs a senior legend).

rubrics_metrics.name: Candor and directness: avoid 'damning with faint praise'
rubrics_metrics.description: Be candid and direct in recommendation letters; if uncomfortable making a positive statement, decline to write rather than produce opaque faint praise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguous or tepid letters burden evaluators with guessing the writer's intent. If letters may be disclosed to candidates, consider whether candor or refusal is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor content to the soliciting institution
rubrics_metrics.description: Adapt letters and evaluations to the institution's priorities (teaching-focused colleges vs research institutions) and speak in the language they want to hear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If solicited by a teaching institution, emphasize teaching, curriculum, and relevant publications; a deep dive into highly recondite research may be less appropriate.
